summary: WebDAV lets clients manage files on web servers, and many such servers limit how much storage can be used. This document defines properties that let a client discover the quota available and the amount used for a collection of resources. It is a standards-track specification meant to help clients and servers interoperate.

eli5.summary: Imagine a locker with a limit on how much you can stuff inside. This lets your computer ask the locker how much room is left and how much you have already used.

questions: how does webdav report disk quota
what does http 507 insufficient storage mean
how to check webdav quota with propfind
subtitle: Two WebDAV properties that let a client see how much storage is left and how much is used.

tldr.problem: WebDAV servers are often deployed with quota limits, but clients had no standard way to learn how much space remained or how much counted against the quota.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two live properties, DAV:quota-available-bytes and DAV:quota-used-bytes, which a client reads with PROPFIND, plus a 507 error with precondition tags when a request would exceed the quota.
tldr.outcome: Clients can show remaining space and avoid running out, though the RFC warns that the numbers rarely match file sizes exactly.

today: RFC 4331 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why WebDAV Needs Quotas
sections.content:
WebDAV servers based on RFC 2518 were already being deployed with quota limits on collections and users. RFC 4331 standardizes that behavior so clients and servers interoperate better.

The RFC gives the usual reasons for quotas: the storage service may charge by quota, the provider may have limited space (such as university student accounts), or managers may want to push users to clean up obsolete files. A client that can see the available and used space has a chance of managing its files before it runs out.
sections.eli5: A school locker can only hold so much. If you can check how full it is, you will not get stuck at the door with a backpack that will not fit.

sections.title: Solution Overview
sections.content:
The approach is to define two live properties. A server meets the specification by implementing both DAV:quota-available-bytes and DAV:quota-used-bytes on collections only.

A DAV:allprop PROPFIND request SHOULD NOT return either property. Their names MUST be returned in a DAV:propname request for a resource that supports them, except in the case of infinite limits. The definitions borrow heavily from the quota definitions in the NFS specification (RFC 3530).
sections.eli5: The server keeps two labels on each folder: one says how much room is left, the other how much is used. You have to ask for them by name.

sections.title: The Two Quota Properties
sections.content:
DAV:quota-available-bytes is the number of octets of additional space that can be allocated to a resource before further allocations are refused. That space may be consumed by other resources. A value of 0 means writes such as a PUT inside a collection will probably fail, though overwriting an existing resource of equal size may still work. If several overlapping limits exist, the server may choose any of them but SHOULD do so in a repeatable way, for example by choosing the smallest number.

DAV:quota-used-bytes is the number of octets used by the resource and possibly other similar resources, where allocating to any of them counts against DAV:quota-available-bytes. It MUST include usage derived from sub-resources where appropriate, and SHOULD include metadata storage if that counts against the quota.

Both are REQUIRED on collections and OPTIONAL on other resources. A server SHOULD implement each on every resource that has the other. If there is no quota or storage is unlimited, a server MAY omit quota-available-bytes (a 404 Not Found in the Multi-Status response), although the RFC recommends returning a value such as the free disk space.

Both values cannot be written by clients. Attempts to write them should get a 403 Forbidden response, with an XML error body using the DAV:cannot-modify-protected-property precondition.
sections.eli5: One number says how many crayons are left in the box, the other says how many you have used. You can look at the numbers but you cannot change them yourself.

sections.title: Example PROPFIND Exchange
sections.content: The RFC shows a client sending a PROPFIND with Depth: 0 for /~milele/public/, asking for both properties by name. The server answers 207 Multi-Status with 596650 for quota-available-bytes and 403350 for quota-used-bytes, each inside a 200 OK propstat.
sections.eli5: You ask the folder, "How much room is left and how much is used?" and it answers with two numbers.

sections.title: Error Reporting
sections.content:
WebDAV already defines status code 507 (Insufficient Storage). It SHOULD be used when a request such as PUT, PROPFIND, MKCOL, MOVE or COPY fails because it would exceed the quota or physical storage limits. To tell this apart from other storage problems, the server SHOULD include an XML error body with a precondition tag.

Two preconditions are defined: DAV:quota-not-exceeded (the request MUST NOT cause the allocated quota to be exceeded) and DAV:sufficient-disk-space (there is enough physical space to run the request). The RFC notes that clients may map these to operating system codes such as E_NOSPC and E_DQUOT in NFS.
sections.eli5: If the locker is full, the server does not just say no. It says whether your own limit ran out or the whole building is out of space.

sections.title: Why the Numbers Do Not Add Up
sections.content:
Servers account for storage in many ways: some skip metadata, some keep older versions, variants of a resource may differ in length, content may be generated on the fly or compressed, and some resources may be stored for free. So clients should expect that:

  • A file's size on the client, or in a PUT, may not match the storage the server needs, so the client cannot predict with 100% accuracy whether a file will fit.
  • Deleting or overwriting may not free the amount shown by DAV:getcontentlength, for example because the file went to a trash folder or was retained by a versioning system.
  • Clients should not assume DAV:quota-used-bytes equals the sum of DAV:getcontentlength for the members of a collection.
  • With user-based quotas, quota-used-bytes will usually be the same for a collection and its members.
  • Where quota is counted by collection, a sub-collection may have a larger quota than its parent. In the RFC's example, /~milele/ has 100 MB and /~milele/public/ is unlimited.
sections.eli5: The locker might count a box of old toys differently than you do, or keep a copy in the recycle bin. So its numbers will not always match your own count.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
The security section is short. An attacker may prefer to store files in collections with a large quota, but the RFC says this is not strictly a security concern because it does not make storing files any easier. On the other hand, DAV:quota-used-bytes may make it easier to detect tampering or misuse.

For internationalization, quota is counted in Arabic numerals expressed as strings, so the RFC says there are no internationalization considerations.
sections.eli5: Someone might hide stuff in the biggest locker, but seeing how full a locker is can help you notice something odd.
